# Chapter 20 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) (a) Qualitative - screening many risks fast is the workhorse's job;
numbers on forty fresh risks would be forty guesses. (b) Quantitative - the
decision is money against money, so an expected-loss comparison (with ranges) is
the persuasive form. (c) Qualitative - a newcomer needs the clear picture: The
matrix, the top risks, the trend; precision would obscure. (2) Before:
$1 \times 30\text{k} =$ EUR 30k/yr. After: $0.2 \times 30\text{k} =$ EUR 6k/yr.
Benefit: EUR 24k/yr against EUR 8k cost - clear yes. Honest version: Outages
"roughly once a year, EUR 20--50k each" give EUR 20--50k/yr falling to about
EUR 4--10k/yr; the protection pays for itself across the whole range, which is
what makes the decision robust rather than precise. (3) Where do $P$ and $V$
come from - which incidents, whose data? What range sits behind the point
estimate - and why are there six significant figures? What would change the
number - which assumptions is it most sensitive to? Expected instead:
"Expected annual loss is roughly EUR 250--450k, driven mainly by the assumed
breach frequency; assumptions attached." (4) Levels 5$\to$`<!-- -->`{=html}1:
EUR 1 M, 100k, 10k, 1k, 100. R3 at EUR 400k sits between levels 4 and 5 on money
- rated impact 5 on this scale (nearest band; on a 10 M scale it was a 4),
which itself demonstrates that levels are scale-relative and must be read with
their table. (5) Example: R1 (post-MFA) level 2 likelihood, level 3--4 impact
$\to$ every 20 years, EUR 10--100k $\to$ expected loss well under EUR 5k/yr; R2
level 3--4 likelihood, level 3 impact $\to$ EUR 15--50k/yr; R3 level 2--3
likelihood, level 4--5 impact $\to$ EUR 20--200k/yr. New conclusion: The
register can be *summed* - total expected loss on the order of EUR 50--250k a
year - a security budget anchor no set of colour-coded levels could provide.
